source.title: A Non-Asymptotic Class of Dense Precision Matrix Estimators: Complexity, Signal and Double Descent
source.citation: Mehmet Caner Agostino Capponi Maurizo Daniele Mihailo Stojnic, 2025
source.authors: Mehmet Caner Agostino Capponi Maurizo Daniele Mihailo Stojnic

page_placements.theme: Portfolio and forecasting objectives can behave differently across capacity

record.tranche_reason: The study measures double-descent-like changes in precision-matrix estimation error across dimensionality using ridgeless regression, a different setting and measure from the original deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's simulations and figures report the study's own estimation-error results across p. Table 1 varies n and p jointly at fixed ratios, rather than tracing a curve through the interpolation threshold; Table 2 and Tables C.4-C.5 report quantities used to discuss the mechanism, not error outcomes. The paper's Sharpe-ratio pattern is recorded separately as a related but different outcome. Cited results from other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps outcome dimensionality p at fixed n=200 for a ridgeless (minimum-norm) precision-matrix estimator, a non-deep model class. It reports whether estimation error falls again past the interpolation point p≈n, which bears on V4 in a new setting. The method is not aimed at deep networks, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that their RRE estimator can exhibit double descent in precision-matrix estimation error as p grows relative to n. The theory establishes the possibility, not a proof of a non-monotone curve. Simulations show the pattern under two noise designs, and it disappears when tr(ΣU)/n is held constant. The Sharpe-ratio 'double ascent' is illustrative only.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses ridgeless regression for precision-matrix estimation and sweeps outcome dimensionality in simulated factor-model data; it does not use deep networks or measure their test error.
record.method_sensitivity: The estimation-error pattern changes across idiosyncratic-noise specifications: it remains in the baseline and first alternative and disappears when tr(ΣU)/n = 2.

fits_no_version.finding: RRE out-of-sample GMV-portfolio Sharpe ratio goes 0.550 (p=10), −0.103 (p=100), 0.631 (p=200). Portfolio composition and target change with p.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream portfolio performance of an interpolating estimator can be non-monotone in portfolio size across the p=n_in threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors attribute the post-interpolation descent to growth of δn=min tr(ΣU,−j)/n with p. Growing noise trace in the regressors acts like implicit shrinkage. When δn stays flat, the descent vanishes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ridgeless regression with noisy regressors, the second descent depends on regressor-noise trace growing with dimension.

record.problems: The plotted estimation-error curves do not provide tabulated values or stated uncertainty intervals. The alternative-noise experiments change data-generating conditions and are described by the authors as descriptive, not proof that δn alone causes the pattern. The portfolio-size comparison changes portfolio composition and target, and its Sharpe-ratio results are not direct estimation-error evidence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional error-curve results were reported as numerical values in text or tables. Table 1 varies sample size and p jointly at fixed ratios and does not trace the interpolation curve; Table 2 and Tables C.4-C.5 list theoretical-rate quantities rather than error outcomes.

untested.parts: No deep networks; no model-size sweep of neural test error.
Sample size is not varied at fixed p near the interpolation threshold. Table 1 scales n and p jointly at fixed ratios.
No single effective-complexity measure is shown to predict the peak location across axes.
Idiosyncratic noise is varied, but this changes the second descent, not the peak. No test of label noise driving the peak, multiple or split peaks, or tuned regularization removing the peak.
No re-expression of capacity via an effective parameter count.

missing.what: RRE max row-wise l2 error is much lower at p=3n/2 than at p=n/2 for every n and K. For example, K=3, n=100: 0.5811 vs 0.1947. The same holds with t-distributed errors. This is tabulated evidence that the overparameterized side beats the underparameterized side.

record.verdict_notes: V6 links were removed from r1–r3. The manipulated noise affects whether the second descent occurs, via δn. V6 instead concerns label noise driving the peak and optimal regularization removing it, so its untested parts should not become verdicts. The error curves are figure-only, on a log scale, with no uncertainty shown. The study is a preprint with no stated code.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error as model size grows.
Changing training-sample size near the interpolation threshold.
The study tests dimensionality-dependent estimation error for its RRE precision-matrix estimator, not risk curves across a broad range of model classes or the classical U-shaped curve generally.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
The study varies idiosyncratic-noise specifications, but does not test label noise, multiple or split peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
No re-expression of the curve using an effective parameter count is tested.

rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of outcomes p across p ∈ {20, 50, 100, 200, 300, 500, 1000} at n = 200 and K = 3; measured maximum absolute linear-combination estimation error.

conditions.value: Baseline: diagonal entries of ΣU drawn independently from Unif(1, 3) × log(p)

rows.measure: Maximum absolute linear-combination estimation error of the RRE precision matrix estimator
rows.note: The authors describe the simulation pattern as double descent. They discuss the interpolation region and say the error falls again beyond it; plotted values are not tabulated.
rows.check: V6 link removed. The baseline sweep shows error rising toward p≈n=200 and falling again for p>n (Figure 1, log scale). It does not test whether label noise drives the peak, whether peaks split, or whether the peak vanishes under optimal regularization. The measure is precision-matrix estimation error, not test risk, and its values are figure-only.

tranche.reason: The study tests double descent in a new setting: dense precision-matrix estimation using ridgeless regressions, with its own dimensionality sweeps and estimation-error results.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v3, September 2026, despite the record's 2025 year. The authors' conclusion is accurately qualified: theory establishes possibility, simulations compare changing data-generating processes, and portfolio Sharpe ratios are illustrative.

statements.correction: n=200; K=3; baseline variances Unif(1,3)×log(p); first alternative variances Unif(0.1,0.3); double descent reported in Figure 1 and Appendix C.1; 500 simulation replications specified in Section 5.1; no standard errors, confidence intervals or uncertainty bands reported for the estimation-error curves.
statements.problem: The double-descent result and simulation conditions are supported, but the claim that precision estimation reports uncertainty is unsupported for these curves.
